edition: Discover — 20 November 2026 · Shadows, Stories and Last Things
intro: A phantom coach, a new UFO-observation proposal and a warehouse of uncanny inheritances open this edition. Explore gothic and fairytale gaming, an Orthodox discussion of hell, the Fathers on Proverbs and the fall of the Mad King. All selections are from November; the Chiller review and Wolf Among Us piece revisit older works. The complete story retains its issue-month date, and substantial spoilers are flagged.

items.title: Avi Loeb heads up plan for new observatory to directly image UFOs
items.summary: A report on a proposed Ithaca observatory combining radar, automated screening and a telescope to capture images and spectra of unidentified aerial objects. The project is an attempt to collect better observations; it has not established an extraterrestrial explanation.
items.why: For your Why Files-style curiosity, the appeal is how an elusive sighting could become something measurable. It gives you an investigation to follow beyond testimony and declassified anecdotes.

items.title: The Warehouse of Exiled Things
items.summary: A complete 4,584-word story from Nightmare’s November issue. A woman returning to Shanghai retrieves an unsettling inheritance from a warehouse for things the city has rejected. A mysterious child and a jade stone lead into memory, belonging and the parts of ourselves we cast away.
items.why: A proper evening’s fiction rather than another reading recommendation: an eerie place with its own rules, an uncanny companion and an emotional mystery beneath the supernatural surface.

items.title: Curse of Resthaven
items.summary: Mark Roddison reviews a narrative adventure RPG set in a troubled island colony. Six-day loops combine questioning residents, managing trade and card-based expeditions into a landscape of bleeding trees and cosmic dread. He praises its atmosphere and interconnected stories while noting that later loops can lose momentum. Contains premise and mechanics spoilers.
items.why: An especially close match for your horror and RPG interests: a mystery you unravel through people, schedules and dangerous journeys, with gloomy art doing as much work as the monsters.

items.title: Why Some People Leave Christianity Over the "Problem of Hell"
items.summary: A 104-minute Orthodox apologetics discussion about hell, eternal judgment and why these doctrines can become obstacles to Christian belief. Cassian King presents an Orthodox response to the problem in the context of final things.
items.why: A substantial session for your interest in salvation and competing Christian interpretations of the afterlife. Its explicitly Orthodox perspective gives you a useful account to compare with Catholic and other theological arguments.
items.source: Ancient Faith / The Orthodox Apologetics Podcast

items.title: The Ghosts of Hatfield House, Hertfordshire
items.summary: A historical haunting survey led by the Cecil family’s phantom coach, recorded in Victorian accounts and said to climb a staircase before disappearing. It distinguishes those traceable stories from less well-sourced modern claims about Elizabeth I. The page is dated 5 November, although its footer carries an earlier update date.
items.why: A haunting with layers to investigate: the strange carriage is memorable, but so is the chance to see how a documented family story acquires extra ghosts over time.

items.title: A Guide to the Proverbial Life
items.summary: Henry T. Edmondson III explores Proverbs through wisdom, speech, humility and prudence, bringing in Augustine, Ambrose and Chrysostom. He considers how adjacent verses can give apparently opposite advice when different situations call for different responses.
items.why: For your interest in reading Scripture with the Fathers, this connects symbolic interpretation with practical judgment. The discussion of apparent contradictions offers something more substantial than isolated inspirational verses.
items.source: Word on Fire / Henry T. Edmondson III

items.title: The Wolf Among Us Remastered
items.summary: A fresh review and retrospective on Telltale’s dark fairytale detective adventure. Tom Naylor revisits Fabletown’s atmosphere, compromised institutions and difficult choices, then weighs the remaster’s redesigned visuals and mixed bonus material. Contains story and character spoilers.
items.why: Fairytale figures behaving like the inhabitants of a morally messy fantasy city should suit your taste for layered worlds. It also points toward the Fables comics if you want to follow the setting onto the page.

items.title: Chiller (1995): Number Six TV REVIEW
items.summary: A new retrospective on the 1995 anthology’s final episode, in which a detective faces child murders timed to the full moon and an ominous schoolyard game. Richard Markworth examines its combination of police thriller and supernatural folk horror. Major episode spoilers; includes discussion of violence against children.
items.why: A less obvious British horror discovery, with ordinary streets and playground rituals becoming threatening. The review offers a route into an older anthology if atmospheric unease appeals more than spectacle.

items.title: Everydayness and the Search Beyond
items.summary: Daniel Fitzpatrick connects Walker Percy, Dante, Tim Gautreaux and composer Alma Deutscher in an essay about losing and recovering wonder. Literature and music become ways to examine grace, moral awakening and the transformation of familiar things. Contains substantial plot spoilers for Gautreaux’s Waiting for the Evening News.
items.why: A bridge between your theology and literary interests, with several authors to explore afterwards. Its movement from Dante’s strange journey to music made from city sirens is an unexpected pairing worth reading.

items.category: A Song of Ice and Fire lore
items.title: The Mad King: Robert’s Rebellion
items.summary: History of Westeros examines Robert’s Rebellion through The Mad King stage play, discussing the Trident, King’s Landing, Lyanna and the Tower of Joy alongside the conflict’s beginnings. The hosts offer both favourite moments and criticisms of the adaptation. Major ASOIAF and stage-play spoilers.
items.why: For the Westeros history that invites competing readings of motives and remembered events. It follows the rebellion itself, complementing the earlier Harrenhal pick while giving you a different adaptation’s choices to weigh.
